title: Dependent Origination, Brain, and Evolution
summary: Dependent origination is a conceptual description of conditional, interdependent arising; the brain is a biological system whose evolution and moment-to-moment activity exploit and embody those conditional relations, without invoking anything outside physical processes.

content_html:
Dependent Origination, Brain, and Evolution

In classical Buddhist thought, dependent origination (Pali: paṭicca-samuppāda, Sanskrit: pratītya-samutpāda) is the principle that phenomena arise only in dependence on conditions. Nothing exists or persists as a self-sufficient, independent entity; instead, things come to be, change, and cease as part of interdependent causal networks. In early formulations, this is often expressed through the twelvefold chain that links ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death as mutually conditioning processes in the life of a sentient being.

From a neuroscientific point of view, the brain is not a self-contained, detached controller but a highly plastic, continuously updating system that is deeply dependent on sensory input, bodily states, social context, and prior learning. Contemporary frameworks such as predictive processing and the free-energy principle describe the brain as an organ that constantly adjusts its internal models to reduce prediction error relative to incoming signals, across multiple levels of a hierarchical generative model. In this sense, brain function is inherently relational: perception, cognition, and emotion emerge from ongoing interactions between organism and environment rather than from an isolated, inner essence.

This dynamic dependence resonates with the spirit of dependent origination. Neural activity patterns do not simply appear out of nowhere; they arise from the interaction of many conditions: evolutionary history, developmental pathways, synaptic plasticity, present sensory input, bodily signals, and current social and cultural context. The sense of a stable, independent self that “has” thoughts can, in this view, be understood as a constructed summary of many conditional processes distributed across brain, body, and world.

Alignment Through Physical Evolution

Evolution by natural selection shapes organisms to track and exploit regularities in their environments. Over deep time, nervous systems have evolved architectures that make use of conditional dependencies in the world: if certain cues reliably precede food, danger, or social opportunities, brains that build internal models of those dependencies gain a fitness advantage. This leads to predictive, model-based control where behaviour is guided by learned and inherited patterns of conditional expectation.

On one reading, this means that the brain is “aligned” with dependent origination in the modest sense that it is an engine for exploiting the fact that the world is structured by conditional relations rather than isolated events. The higher-level regularities that Buddhism points to philosophically (no independent self, conditioned arising of suffering, etc.) and the functional regularities that neuroscience uncovers (hierarchical prediction, context-sensitive plasticity, multi-level feedback loops) both describe a reality in which stable patterns emerge from networks of conditions rather than from fixed essences.

Bridging Conceptual and Neural Levels

There is no need to posit an extra, non-physical system for dependent origination to be relevant to the brain. Instead, it can be seen as a conceptual lens for understanding the kinds of interdependence that modern neuroscience and evolutionary theory already reveal. Meditative practices that emphasise seeing thoughts, feelings, and perceptions as conditioned and transient may, over time, reshape large-scale brain networks (for example, networks involved in self-focused rumination and narrative identity) in ways that are measurable with neuroimaging and consistent with reduced reactivity and increased flexibility.
